The proposed CO operation at T-RICH is not expected to introduce any greater hazards to the surrounding 2 area than these two operations currently do, and in fact T-RICH is likely to present less cumulative risk of harm or loss due to the unique properties of CO . 2 3.7 CONCEPTUAL EMERGENCY RESPONSE PLAN The proposed T-RICH site is near existing port facilities and terminals which regularly handle hazardous materials in their daily operations which could negatively affect the surrounding communities and environment if not adequately addressed, and lessons can and should be utilized from these existing Page34 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version terminal operators who have safely managed these risks when crafting the emergency response plans for T-RICH. Perhaps the most hazardous material handled in the port with the highest potential negative impact to the area is anhydrous ammonia, which has been dubbed one of the region’s most dangerous chemicals. Approximately two million tons per year are imported into Tampa via ship from an ammonia production facility in Donaldsonville, Louisiana, for use in the production of ammoniated phosphate fertilizer. West- central Florida produces roughly 75% of the nation’s phosphate. It is then piped in liquid form from the port to inland facilities like Mosaic’s Bartow and New Wales plants via a 75-mile underground pipeline where ammoniated phosphate fertilizer is made with the phosphates mined in the area. Anhydrous ammonia is classified by the EPA as an Extremely Hazardous Substance (EHS). The port houses two such ammonia handling facilities, one 1.3 miles northwest on Hooker’s Point, and the other only 700 feet away directly across the shipping channel from the T-RICH site. A study of these and a third nearby terminal was funded by the EPA in 1995 to identify existing hazards and response capabilities and to make recommendations for local first responders and other affected groups. This study was cited in the Tampa Bay Hazardous Materials Emergency Response Plan, dated June 202014. The following is a brief summary of some of their findings: 1. Improved warnings to the public in the event of accidental release. In 1999 a siren warning and telephone ring-down system was installed to inform residents adjacent to Port Tampa Bay of an unintended release. The coverage area was expanded from an initial one-mile radius to a ten-mile radius with additional sirens installed. The ring-down system notifies all tenants of the Port as well as schools, churches, other public facilities, and certain private residences who chose to register their numbers. The sirens include pre-recorded or live voice capability. It is highly possible that the T-RICH site will incorporate a similar audible and telephone warning system, or perhaps even piggy-back off this existing system. 2. Periodic safety meetings between the ammonia terminal operators and local stakeholders.
